intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene on chromosome 17p12-q12.

checks.claim: Nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Our discovery of two additional TMEM98 mutations confirms the important role of the gene in the pathogenesis of autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.
checks.explanation: The paper attributes autosomal dominant nanophthalmos to TMEM98 mutations, and the deletion is explicitly heterozygous. The NNO4 designation is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The TMEM98 gene is located on chromosome 17p12-q12.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation in TMEM98 in a large white kindred with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos linked to 17p12-q12.
checks.explanation: TMEM98 lies within the linked region on 17p12-q12.

paragraphs.text: Nanophthalmos is a congenital disorder in which the eye is small but structurally normal. Its main complications are severe hyperopia and angle-closure glaucoma (Awadalla et al., 2014). Affected individuals also have a higher risk of complications after eye surgery (Khorram et al., 2015). NNO4 is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

checks.claim: Nanophthalmos is a congenital disorder in which the eye is small but structurally normal.
checks.evidence_quote: Nanophthalmos is a congenital disorder characterized by small eyes
checks.explanation: The abstract says the disorder is congenital with small eyes but does not say the eye is 'structurally normal'.

checks.claim: The main complications of nanophthalmos are severe hyperopia and angle-closure glaucoma.
checks.evidence_quote: with the main complications being severe hyperopia and angle-closure glaucoma.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Individuals with nanophthalmos have a higher risk of complications after eye surgery.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients with nanophthalmos have high hyperopia (far-sightedness), a greater incidence of angle-closure glaucoma, and increased risk of surgical complications.

checks.claim: NNO4 is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
checks.evidence_quote: To our knowledge, this represents the first gene identified causing autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.
checks.explanation: Autosomal dominant inheritance is stated. The NNO4 label itself comes from nomenclature, not the paper.

paragraphs.text: Yu et al. (2009) studied a 5-generation Chinese family with simple microphthalmia inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Nine affected members were aged 6 to 66 years (mean, 42.8 years) and had bilateral isolated microphthalmia present from birth. No family members had other physical anomalies. Hyperopia ranged from +4.50 to +11.50 diopters (mean, +8.00 diopters). Axial length ranged from 18.22 mm to 20.26 mm (mean, 19.29 mm). In most eyes, best corrected visual acuity was less than 0.5. Three patients, all older than 50 years, had angle-closure glaucoma or occludable anterior chamber angles. They were treated by trabeculectomy, but the disease continued to progress, and 2 patients developed atrophia bulbi despite repeated surgeries. On histology, collagen fibers in the scleral stroma were diffusely swollen, twisted, or frayed and mixed with normal fibers. In the 2 atrophied globes, the collagen fibers were misaligned and the sclera contained abundant coil-like amorphous material and was 3 times the normal thickness. The corneas in these globes were also thickened, pigment cells had proliferated, and bone-like tissue had formed. Karyotypes were normal in all 9 affected members. In their discussion, Yu et al. (2009) noted learning disabilities in one-third of the cases.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) studied a large white family (NNO-SA1) from South Australia with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Nanophthalmos was defined as an axial length of less than 20.0 mm and/or a refractive error greater than +7.00. Of 35 available family members, 16 (46%) were diagnosed with nanophthalmos. Their mean refraction was +11.8 D and their mean axial length was 17.6 mm.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) reported 2 large families with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos showing high penetrance over at least 4 generations. The first family (991-F) was white, of German heritage, and lived in the United States. Six of 10 examined members had nanophthalmos, and 3 more were affected by family history. Mean axial eye length in the available patients was 17.1 +/- 0.31 mm. Mean spherical equivalent refraction was +13.0 +/- 0.89 diopters, compared with +0.71 +/- 0.81 diopters in unaffected members. The second family (951-N) was a Pacific Islander family of Micronesian heritage from the Mariana Islands. Eight of 10 examined members had nanophthalmos, with a mean axial eye length of 17.4 +/- 0.94 mm, compared with 22.7 +/- 0.38 mm in unaffected members. Their mean spherical equivalent refraction was +3.93 +/- 1.57 diopters. Three more members of this family were affected by family history. Across both families, axial eye length in affected individuals ranged from 15.9 to 18.4 mm.

The highest 2-point LOD score was 4.97 at D17S1824 (recombination fraction 0.00). Haplotype analysis placed the disease gene in a 21.57-cM interval between D17S900 and D17S1872 on chromosome 17p12-q12.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) performed exome sequencing in the large white Australian family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos linked to chromosome 17p12-q12. Within the linked region they identified a single novel segregating missense variant, a heterozygous c.577G-C transversion in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene that results in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. The variant was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls. RT-PCR showed TMEM98 expression in all ocular tissues tested, including sclera and optic nerve head.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) performed exome sequencing in an affected member of family 991-F. Within the chromosome 17 linked region, they found a heterozygous his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in TMEM98. Sanger sequencing showed that all other affected family members carried the mutation and that it was absent from unaffected members. Sanger sequencing of TMEM98 in family 951-N identified a heterozygous 34-bp deletion (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg) in all affected family members, and it was absent from healthy members. The deletion spans the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4. It removes a splice site and results in premature termination of translation. Neither mutation was found in the Exome Variant Server or the 1000 Genomes Project.

paragraphs.text: Awadalla et al. (2014) studied a large white Australian family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. In affected members they identified a heterozygous c.577G-C transversion in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene, resulting in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. The mutation was found by exome sequencing within a region of chromosome 17 linked to the disease, and it segregated with the disease in the family. It was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) studied a white family from the United States (991-F) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. In affected members they identified a heterozygous his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in the TMEM98 gene. The mutation was found by exome sequencing within a linked region on chromosome 17p12-q12 and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It was present in all affected family members and absent from healthy members. The mutation was predicted to be damaging by SIFT, PolyPhen, and BLOSUM62, alters a histidine conserved across species, and was absent from the Exome Variant Server and 1000 Genomes Project databases.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) studied a Pacific Islander family of Micronesian heritage from the Mariana Islands (951-N) with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Sanger sequencing identified a heterozygous 34-bp deletion in the TMEM98 gene (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg) in all affected family members. The deletion spans the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4, removes a splice site, and results in premature termination of translation. It was absent from healthy family members and from the Exome Variant Server and 1000 Genomes Project databases.
